title: VeDi 2025
text:
Overview
VeDi 2025 is an Italian Ministry of Economic Development (MISE) funded research project between Centro Ricerche Fiat (CRF, Stellantis) and the University of Trento, evaluating motion planning approaches in a real Stellantis test vehicle. It uses V2X (vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure) communication enabled by the roadside infrastructure installed on the Brennero highway, and also covers deploying neural networks directly on the car's experimental ECU. Part of the work is directly tied to my PhD.

title: VeDi 2025
text:
Two planners
Stellantis wanted two independent planners evaluated in the same vehicle architecture:

CODRIVER - an existing planner developed by Prof. Mauro Da Lio and collaborators during the European project DREAM4CARS, adapted by UniTN for this use case.
MPTree - a sampling-based planner built from scratch by me, under the supervision of Prof. Francesco Biral. It is derived from RRT*, but exploits prior knowledge of the road geometry to shrink the exploration domain and reach real-time performance - not standard practice for RRT-based planning in robotics - and connects nodes with optimal motion primitives and clothoids instead of straight lines.

title: VeDi 2025
text:
Development path

MATLAB MVP to validate the core planning approach.
The MVP grew into the VehiclePrimitives library.
C++ port, tested standalone and integrated with the commercial simulator IPG CarMaker.
SIL and HIL testing on an experimental ECU (dSPACE AUTERA) replaying real car logs.
VIL testing in the real vehicle, at the Vadena safety test site and at Stellantis's Balocco proving ground.

title: VeDi 2025
text:
Maneuver negotiation
Alongside single-vehicle planning, the project required decentralized negotiation between agents. Vehicles exchange over V2X not just their current state but their currently committed maneuver, so two vehicles can plan an intersection crossing, overtake, or cut-in jointly rather than reactively. A vehicle can also broadcast a desired maneuver that differs from its committed one; the receiving agent folds this into its own tree search, biasing both expansion and cost function toward a maneuver that works for both. The scheme is decentralized and emergent, based on mutual penalization and biasing rather than a central negotiator.

title: VeDi 2025
text:
Publication
MPTree: A Sampling-based Vehicle Motion Planner for Real-time Obstacle Avoidance (IFAC-PapersOnLine, 2024) - also covered in a chapter of my PhD thesis.

Overview
A browser-based CSV/TSV scope viewer for telemetry and logs. Open a data file and plot its columns as time series, XY, or XYZ - no build step, no dependencies, nothing leaves the machine it runs on. Built for the same kind of quick, throwaway telemetry inspection that usually ends up in a one-off Python script, except it stays open in a browser tab and needs nothing installed.

title: scope
text:
Why a browser tool
Most telemetry from simulation runs or vehicle logs is a CSV of time-stamped channels, and the fastest way to look at it shouldn't require opening a notebook or writing a plotting script. Because it's a static page with no server component, the same file works as a local double-click tool and as a hosted page - the file itself never has to leave the machine.

title: geographic_coordinates
text:
Overview
A small library for converting between the three coordinate frames that show up constantly in vehicle localization: geodetic coordinates (latitude/longitude/height, what a GNSS receiver hands you), Earth-Centered- Earth-Fixed (ECEF) coordinates, and a local East-North-Up (ENU) frame - built on the WGS84 ellipsoid, the datum GPS itself uses.

title: geographic_coordinates
text:
Why it exists
Raw GNSS output is geodetic and effectively unusable directly for local motion planning or control - a change in latitude near the equator covers a different physical distance than the same change near a pole, and the numbers don't behave like a flat Cartesian frame at all. This library anchors a local ENU frame at a chosen origin and converts to and from it, so downstream code can work in plain, locally-flat meters instead of degrees of latitude and longitude.

title: geographic_coordinates
text:
Interface
A C++ core with a thin Python binding layer (via a C API), so the same tested conversion code is usable from either language without maintaining two implementations.

title: geographic_coordinates
text:
Status
Public C++/Python library, ongoing personal project.

title: About
text:
I grew up wanting to know why things move the way they do. That curiosity eventually became a PhD: I build algorithms that find the fastest way a vehicle can move without asking for more grip than it has. I'm a PhD candidate in the Doctoral Program in Materials, Mechatronics and Systems Engineering (DRMMSE) at the University of Trento, where my days split between optimal control theory, C++, and convincing a solver to converge.
The common thread across everything I have worked on - minimum lap time simulation, real-time velocity planning, maneuver negotiation for self-driving cars - is the same question asked at different scales: given the physics a vehicle actually has, what is the fastest, safest thing it can do right now, and can the answer arrive fast enough to be useful. Off the clock, I trade the desk for a mountain: climbing, skiing, mountain biking, or grilling for whoever is around.

title: FBGA
text:
<- All projects
Personal project, developed during the PhD | 2025 - present

title: FBGA
text:
Overview
FBGA - Forward-Backward Generic Acceleration constraints - computes the maximum-performance velocity profile along a path given a complex g-g-v constraint envelope: the combined longitudinal/lateral acceleration limits a vehicle can actually sustain, which change with speed and aren't a simple circle or ellipse. Given a path's curvature profile and that envelope, the forward-backward algorithm finds the fastest velocity profile that never asks the vehicle for more grip than it has, running fast enough for real-time use rather than offline-only optimization. Existing forward-backward planners get their speed by assuming a simple (typically convex) shape for the g-g-v envelope so they can pre-compute the apexes to build the profile around; FBGA instead locates the switching points adaptively while it propagates the solution, so it needs no assumption at all about the envelope's shape - it treats it as a black box that can be evaluated point by point, whether it comes from a formula, a lookup table, or a high-fidelity vehicle model.

title: FBGA
text:
Accuracy and speed
Validated against an indirect optimal control solver (Pins) across five racetracks and two vehicle classes (race car, motorcycle), the 2D solver matches lap times to within roughly 0.1-0.4%, while running up to three orders of magnitude faster - down to fractions of a millisecond per query, well within budget for online, onboard planning. Within a 300 m receding horizon representative of a moving-horizon planner, it solves in a fraction of a millisecond regardless of mesh size, against several milliseconds for the OCP.

title: FBGA
text:
From 2D to 3D
The library started as a 2D solver - curvature-only path, single g-g envelope - published as Real-Time Velocity Profile Optimization for Time-Optimal Maneuvering With Generic Acceleration Constraints (IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, 2025). It has since grown a 3D solver, generic over the vehicle's g-g-v model, that accounts for banked and pitched paths (Suzuka, Laguna Seca, Yas Marina), load transfer, spatially variable grip, and yellow-flag deceleration limits - published as Beyond the Apex: Online Minimum-Time Velocity Planning on Three-Dimensional Paths With Variable Friction (IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, 2026). Unlike prior 3D forward-backward methods, it drops the assumption that a maneuver's apex sits at the geometric corner apex, computing it adaptively instead - within 0.2-0.3% of an OCP baseline and up to 44x faster than the closest prior forward-backward method, while eliminating the g-g-v violations (up to several percent) that apex precomputation causes on tracks with pronounced 3D geometry. It also natively handles non-convex envelopes, such as a motorcycle's no-wheeling/no-stoppie limits, which the super-elliptical formulation used by prior 3D methods cannot represent. The 3D solver was originally developed as its own repository, FBGA_3D, and is now ported into FBGA itself as an opt-in module.

title: FBGA
text: Video explanation

title: FBGA
text:
Related publications

Real-Time Velocity Profile Optimization for Time-Optimal Maneuvering With Generic Acceleration Constraints, IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, 2025 - the original 2D FBGA paper.
Beyond the Apex: Online Minimum-Time Velocity Planning on Three-Dimensional Paths With Variable Friction, IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, 2026 - the 3D extension.

Two more papers building on FBGA are set to appear in their conference proceedings:

Fast GGV-Compliant Sampling-Based Planning for Vehicles, presented at AVEC 2026 (Tsukuba, Japan) - a JSAE Best Paper Award finalist. FBGA is used here as the trajectory-evaluation module inside a sampling-based planner running on a scaled autonomous racing vehicle.








Trajectory Planning and Control near the Limits: an Open Experimental Benchmark on the RoboRacer Platform, IEEE ITSC 2026 (Naples) - an open benchmark where FBGA runs as the real-time velocity re-planner on the same scaled platform, in a different architectural role from the AVEC application.

title: FBGA
text:
Where it runs
Used in the TUM Autonomous Vehicle Systems Laboratory's Indy Autonomous Challenge and Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League entries, where it was benchmarked directly against the velocity planner the team actually races with - not an academic baseline.

title: FBGA
text:
Adoption
Beyond my own use, FBGA has drawn interest from outside its original domain, all through unsolicited contact:

A TUM group working on uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) inquired about applying it to thrust/attitude envelopes, which are similarly non-convex and state-dependent.
A conversation with an Italian industrial vehicle manufacturer at IEEE ICRA 2026 about a possible collaboration, still exploratory.
An ongoing collaboration with Philipp Braun's group (CIICADA Lab, Australian National University) has a joint paper in preparation.

The library is also distributed as an installable Python package, which lowers the bar for anyone to try it without going through a prior agreement.

title: Minimum Lap Time Simulator
text:
Overview
An offline, optimal-control minimum lap time (MLT) simulator developed with Aprilia Racing for MotoGP. Given a track and a vehicle model, the simulator computes the fastest theoretically achievable lap and the full state and control trajectory that achieves it, rather than integrating a driver model forward in time like a traditional lap-time simulator. The project is a direct spinoff of my master's thesis.

title: Minimum Lap Time Simulator
text:
Approach
The motorcycle is modeled as a full multibody system (around 30 states), including a Magic-Formula-based tyre model (MF-MCTyre) and CFD-derived aerodynamic maps, and the minimum-time problem is solved as an indirect optimal control problem. The modeling framework was developed in Maple, with C++ used for the custom classes, models, and solver integration. The boundary-value problem arising from the indirect method is solved with PINS, a specialized indirect optimal control solver developed by Prof. Enrico Bertolazzi, Prof. Francesco Biral, and Prof. Paolo Bosetti - closed source and under license, but available to academia free upon request. Because the problem is numerically stiff and sensitive to the initial guess, the solver uses homotopy continuation - it solves a sequence of progressively harder problems, using each solution as the initial guess for the next, rather than attempting to solve the full nonlinear problem from a cold start.

title: Minimum Lap Time Simulator
text:
Output
Beyond the lap time itself, the simulator produces the full optimal state and control history - speed, lean angle, throttle, brake, tyre loads - which is compared against real telemetry to validate the vehicle model and probe where a rider is leaving performance on the table.

title: Minimum Lap Time Simulator

title: SUNRISE
text:
Overview
SUNRISE - Safety Assurance Framework for Connected and Automated Mobility Systems - is a Horizon Europe project (Grant 101069573) coordinated by Applus IDIADA, with a 25+ partner consortium spanning automotive suppliers (Continental, Infineon, Renault, Toyota), research institutions (Chalmers, University of Warwick), testing organizations (RISE, AVL), and infrastructure bodies (ERTICO, TNO). It builds a harmonized, scalable safety assurance framework for CCAM: generating scenarios from an Operational Design Domain (ODD), allocating them across simulation, X-in-the-loop, and proving grounds, and aggregating microscopic test results into macroscopic safety conclusions, with a federated European scenario data framework, test case library, and handbook as deliverables.

title: SUNRISE
text:
What I worked on
Our contribution is a data-driven framework for quantifiable safety assessment: a stochastic model that predicts safety outcomes (collision, near-miss, safe) for any parametrized driving scenario, with quantified uncertainty, using bootstrap aggregation - an ensemble of compact feed-forward neural networks, each trained on a random sample of the scenario space. Unlike running full simulations, the trained ensemble executes in microseconds, enabling both offline diagnosis and online, real-time decision support.
I applied the framework to MPTree - the planner developed in my PhD - for a full safety assessment and a real-time safe speed recommendation, and to CoDriver's larger simulation dataset for failure mode identification, showing the framework transfers across planning agents without modification. I also developed the two self-driving agents used as systems under test throughout this work: the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) baseline and MPTree/Motion Planner itself.

title: SUNRISE
text:
Applications

Safety assessment - estimating collision probability over hypothetical risk subdomains (e.g. a distracted driver missing the merge, at various relative speeds and maneuver aggressiveness) via fast Monte Carlo evaluation of the trained ensemble.
Failure mode identification - sampling near the learned collision boundary, clustering the resulting near-miss trajectories, and replaying a handful of representative cases per cluster to diagnose specific weaknesses instead of reviewing logs by hand.
Safe speed advisor - an online application that, given the current traffic state, scans candidate ego velocities and recommends the one minimizing collision risk in real time.

title: VehiclePrimitives
text:
Overview
A library of motion primitives for vehicle navigation and control - short, pre-computed maneuver segments (e.g. cubic spiral paths, speed-matched transitions) that a planner can stitch together into a full trajectory instead of solving the whole path from scratch every time. Built to generate feasible trajectories for cars, trucks, and autonomous robots.

title: VehiclePrimitives
text:
MPTreeRRT
The primitives feed an MPTree RRT planner: a sampling-based motion planner that explores the primitive space the way an RRT explores continuous state space, built on the sampling-based approach from the MPTree publication (MPTree: A Sampling-based Vehicle Motion Planner for Real-time Obstacle Avoidance, IFAC-PapersOnLine 2024). Rather than sampling raw control inputs, it samples from the library of dynamically-feasible primitives, which keeps every candidate trajectory kinematically valid by construction.
